General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

Russia is back in world sport, but who is drug testing its athletes?

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (875 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Fresh questions have emerged over Russia's return to world sport after figures reviewed by DW showed that only four of the 16 Russian weightlifters competing at this year's world championships underwent out-of-competition testing by the International Testing Agency (ITA).
  • Two-time European champion Anastasiia Romanova, who previously served a two-year doping ban, was among those not tested by the ITA during the first nine months of 2026, according to its quarterly anti-doping reports.
  • Industry observers note that by comparison, all 13 members of the North Korean team underwent at least one ITA test during the same period.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Fresh questions have emerged over Russia's return to world sport after figures reviewed by DW showed that only four of the 16 Russian weightlifters competing at this year's world championships underwent out-of-competition testing by the International Testing Agency (ITA).

Two-time European champion Anastasiia Romanova, who previously served a two-year doping ban, was among those not tested by the ITA during the first nine months of 2026, according to its quarterly anti-doping reports.

Industry observers note that by comparison, all 13 members of the North Korean team underwent at least one ITA test during the same period. North Korea, like Russia, has a history of doping violations in weightlifting.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The ITA, which runs weightlifting's anti-doping program, told DW that it tested all 16 Russian weightlifters "ahead of their participation in the event." DW understands those tests were conducted in Ningbo, China, where the championships are being held.

In a power sport like weightlifting, performance-enhancing drugs are most beneficial during training, when athletes build strength and muscle mass in the months before competition. Some drugs, such as anabolic steroids, may be harder to detect by the time the competition comes around.

Rob Koehler, head of the athlete-led movement Global Athlete, called the lack of out-of-competition testing "absurd.".

In a recent development, "Out-of-competition testing is the backbone of anti-doping," Koehler told DW. "Everybody knows there's going to be testing at the event. But not everybody knows when they're going to be tested 365 days a year outside events. It's concerning that the ITA doesn't see this as a red flag.".

Marta Nawrocka, the ITA's spokesperson, said that Russian athletes were among the 10 most-tested nationalities in weightlifting this year. She also defended the fact that only two Russian weightlifters feature in the sport's highest-priority testing pool, saying inclusion is based on performance and risk profiles.

"Russia's history of doping in weightlifting remains an important factor in the ITA's risk assessment and testing priorities," Nawrocka noted. "Russian weightlifters remain subject to substantial testing activity.".

Koehler, though, is unconvinced.

"You simply can't treat Russia like any other country," he remarked. "It has to have more scrutiny. It has to have more testing. If you don't do that, you're undermining athlete confidence in the system.".

The International Weightlifting Federation did not respond to a request for comment.

Weightlifting was one of the sports most implicated in Russia's state-sponsored doping scandal, which came to light after the 2014 Sochi Winter Olympics. It ranked second only to athletics for the number of positive cases identified by Canadian lawyer Richard McLaren in his 2016 report commissioned by WADA, the global anti-doping watchdog.

In a recent development, the scandal led to dozens of Russian athletes being banned across numerous sports. RUSADA, Russia's anti-doping agency, has remained suspended for most of the past decade.

As a result, its Moscow laboratory cannot analyze urine and blood samples, meaning samples collected by the agency must be sent abroad for analysis under what WADA described as a "strict chain of custody.".

WADA remarked it continued to monitor RUSADA but had been unable to gain access to the country to review the agency's suspension because of the "ongoing geopolitical situation.".

It added that RUSADA had "collected thousands of samples … including hundreds from weightlifters" so far this year.

It has been revealed that "Given the history, WADA remains vigilant when it comes to Russia," James Fitzgerald, WADA's spokesperson, told DW. "We must ensure that no stone is left unturned when it comes to verifying that all the proper testing and other anti-doping activities are taking place.".

Despite being suspended, RUSADA still has the power to investigate and prosecute anti-doping cases involving Russian athletes, which critics find difficult to reconcile.

"It's a compounding problem that WADA is still giving them a free pass when it can't even get into Russia to see what they're doing," said Koehler, WADA's former deputy director general.

"There's simply no oversight and no accountability. And quite frankly, I don't think there ever really has been.".

Critics also argue that ongoing questions over RUSADA's leadership and independence suggest that little has been fixed in the decade since the McLaren report.

Even the International Olympic Committee (IOC), whose president, Kirsty Coventry, supports the full return of Russian athletes, has acknowledged a "lack of confidence" over RUSADA's governance.

Nawrocka said the IOC had "recently entrusted" the ITA with an expanded role within Russia in the run-up to the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028, but did not explain what the role would involve or when it might begin.

Recent findings suggest that in April, investigative outlet The Insider reported that Veronika Loginova, the agency's head, was in a long-term relationship with an alleged FSB officer. The FSB, Russia's domestic security service, played a central role in covering up positive drug tests at the Sochi Games.

Loginova did not respond to questions for this article but dismissed the allegations at the time as "all this nonsense," writing in an email that she believed "sport exists separate from politics.".

WADA confirmed to DW only that its investigations unit was examining the allegations against Loginova and that the inquiry was ongoing.

  • Fears of curbs on AI data-center spending have added to investors' concerns after Democrats won control of both chambers of the US Congress.
  • Recent findings suggest that the pan-European STOXX 600 index dropped 1.6% in early trading, wiping out its gains for the week.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

European shares fell sharply in early trading on Friday as a global sell-off fueled by concerns over artificial intelligence stocks spread from Wall Street to Asia and Europe.

Fears of curbs on AI data-center spending have added to investors' concerns after Democrats won control of both chambers of the US Congress.

Recent findings suggest that the pan-European STOXX 600 index dropped 1.6% in early trading, wiping out its gains for the week. Most major European markets fell more than 1%, with media, healthcare and retail stocks leading the declines.

European markets had previously weathered the week's turbulence better than their Asian and US counterparts because of their more limited exposure to AI stocks.

Earlier, Japanese and South Korean shares tumbled after a massive selloff in tech stocks on Wall Street the previous day.

Sources indicate that tokyo's benchmark Nikkei 225 index fell 5.5% in early trade, while Seoul's tech-heavy Kospi index slid as much as 8.8%, triggering a circuit breaker which suspended trading for 20 minutes. Taiwan's benchmark TAIEX index was also down more than 8%.

Asian tech giants including Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Firm (TSMC) have borne the brunt of the artificial intelligence-related selloff.

Samsung plunged nearly 10% while SK Hynix slid over 11%.

Chip-related shares in Japan also took a beating, with Tokyo Electron stock trading down around 9% and Kioxia shedding 13%.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

US markets were hammered on Thursday by a sharp retreat in tech stocks, particularly those involved in the buildout of artificial intelligence infrastructure like data centers.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq fell 5.52% and shed as much as $2.5 trillion (roughly €2.23 trillion) in market value, while the broader S&P 500 index plunged 4.4%.

The rout occurred as investors grow increasingly anxious about the colossal AI spending intends and whether they will eventually produce commensurate profits.

The results of the US midterm elections, which saw Democrats seize control of both houses of US Congress, added to the concerns.

A number of Democratic governors-elect campaigned on slowing artificial intelligence development and promised to stop or pause the construction of data centers amid growing public opposition to such projects.

"It's pretty clear there's been a real shift ​in sentiment," Michael McCarthy, chief executive for Australia and Newly introduced Zealand at online brokerage Moomoo, told the Reuters news agency.

Sources indicate that "Market turning points are often accompanied by strong disagreement, and that demonstrates up in the market ​by huge swings in either direction," he remarked. "That's what we appear to have had — and last night's emphatic sell-down suggests that is the direction that we're now headed in.".

Celtic manager Martin O’Neill hailed midfield duo Alex Oxlade-Chamberlain and Luke McCowan after the recalled pair both scored in the 4-1 home win over St Mirren.

With Mika Baur facing 10 weeks out with an ankle injury and Benjamin Nygren nursing a heel problem, O’Neill handed McCowan his second start of the season and Oxlade-Chamberlain his fifth, as the two joined forces for the first time.

Oxlade-Chamberlain and McCowan netted either side of Camilo Duran in a nine-minute flurry of goals late in the first half with Callum McGregor making it four for Celtic in the second period before Killian Phillips reduced the deficit for Saints from the penalty spot.

In a recent development, O’Neill mentioned: ‘Alex has been waiting around for a while to get into the side. He’s a brilliant passer of the ball. He took his goal very well with a calm finish in the bottom corner.

‘He was feeling a little bit sore, so taking him off was just precautionary.

‘I was also delighted Luke got his goal. That should give him a boost in confidence.’.

Oxlade-Chamberlain congratulates McCowan after he scored to make it three for Celtic.

McCowan faced criticism after Celtic’s Champions League collapse against LASK and his only previous start this season saw him taken off at half-time in a home defeat by Rangers.

O’Neill said: ‘I thought he did really well, also playing the full game given it has been some considerable time since he has done that.

According to recent reports, ‘He got the ball early on and played it almost blindly and it was intercepted and I thought, “oh, gosh, here we go”. But he roared back, took his goal well and I am really pleased for him. He is a real genuine lad.

‘It has been tough for him. In the game against Rangers, he was thrown into a position, and it didn’t start well for him in the match. I think he felt it was deja vu for him in terms of the game at the back end of last season too. That will be good for him.’.

The Celtic manager also introduced 19-year-old former PSV Eindhoven midfielder Joel van den Berg for a debut in the second half.

‘I thought he did very well,’ said O’Neill. ‘He’s coming on after an injury which kept him out for some time.

‘I am pleased there is a bit of competition for places now.’.

The veteran midfielder celebrates his strike that opened the scoring against St Mirren.

St Mirren manager Craig McLeish felt Celtic were clinical in his team’s heavy defeat in Glasgow.

‘It’s a really sore one with the way the scoreline ended up,’ stated McLeish.

‘I thought we started the game quite well and then that flurry of goals can happen here when you’re playing against such a strong team. The difference was the quality in our box compared to theirs.

‘They are just so clinical, and they get into those good areas and they punish you.

It has been revealed that ‘I felt we got into some similar areas throughout the game. We didn’t give up, we didn’t move away from what we were trying to do, but we were just really lacking that final bit.’.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Roughly 180 million people could be carrying previously unknown giant viruses inside their guts.
  • Large and giant viruses in the phylum Nucleocytoviricota are a vast group of DNA viruses — some are so major that they can be seen under a light microscope — that mostly infect single-celled organisms in the environment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Many giant viruses can be seen under a light microscope.Credit: Gabrielle Voinot/Eurelios/Look at Sciences/SPL.

Roughly 180 million people could be carrying previously unknown giant viruses inside their guts. Microbiologists say that these ‘egoviruses’ could be the missing link between giant viruses that infect single-celled organisms and distantly related poxviruses, such as those that cause smallpox and mpox, which can infect people and animals directly. The findings are published in Nature1.

Large and giant viruses in the phylum Nucleocytoviricota are a vast group of DNA viruses — some are so major that they can be seen under a light microscope — that mostly infect single-celled organisms in the environment.

In a recent development, poxviruses are an outlier in the giant-virus world because they can directly infect humans and animals and their origin is a mystery, states Fasséli Coulibaly, a structural biologist at Monash University in Melbourne, Australia. Egoviruses could be the evolutionary bridge between microorganism-infecting giant viruses called asfuviruses and pathogenic poxviruses, he says.

It has been revealed that tom Delmont, a microbial ecologist at the French National Centre for Scientific Research in Paris, and his colleagues discovered egoviruses while combing through online libraries of metagenomes. These contain the genetic information of all the organisms in a particular environment, which means that researchers can hunt for microbes without having to cultivate them. When the team scanned for a single gene found in most nucleocytoviruses, they discovered egoviruses — the only type of nucleocytovirus that is prevalent in the gut.

They found egovirus DNA in gut samples from people, buffalo, goats, chickens, deer and pigs. Six clades were unique to people. One of these clades is estimated to be present in roughly 1% of the global population, on the basis of the presence of at least one of two egovirus proteins in the samples they analysed.

In a recent development, the researchers detected these proteins in samples spanning a large proportion of the human population, from the Hadza, a hunter-gatherer group in Tanzania, to populations in Europe, the United States and South America, claims Delmont. That suggests that egoviruses have been inhabiting the human gut for a long time, he adds.

In a recent development, that egoviruses are found in many animal species, including people, and are widespread around the world shows that giant viruses are more diverse than previously thought, indicates Subir Sarker, a molecular virologist at James Cook University in Townsville, Queensland. “This is a really groundbreaking study,” he adds.

Recent findings suggest that to identify potential hosts for egoviruses in the gut, the team compared the amount of genetic overlap between egoviruses and organisms with a nucleus. The researchers found the most overlap with single-celled organisms that help ruminants, such as cows, to digest their food.

Industry News: Exercise coaching boosts colon cancer survival

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In 2025, an international trial found that people treated for colon cancer were more likely to be alive eight years later if they had received long-term exercise coaching.
  • It has been revealed that the question facing doctors now is less whether people with cancer should exercise, and rather how they should build it into routine care.
  • Yet experts caution that the trial's findings may not apply to every cancer or every patient.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In 2025, an international trial found that people treated for colon cancer were more likely to be alive eight years later if they had received long-term exercise coaching.

It has been revealed that the question facing doctors now is less whether people with cancer should exercise, and rather how they should build it into routine care. In the US, that shift is reaching hospital standards. From January 2027, breast cancer centers must screen patients' physical function and recommend exercise or physical therapy where needed.

Yet experts caution that the trial's findings may not apply to every cancer or every patient.

The 2025 trial, called CHALLENGE, was led by the Canadian Cancer Trials Group. It began enrolling patients in 2009 and published its results in 2025.

According to recent reports, the trial's 889 participants came from six countries, most from Canada and Australia. All had finished surgery and chemotherapy for stage 2 or 3 colon cancer, which had not spread to distant organs.

It has been revealed that half received only health education materials on exercise and healthy eating. The other half additionally met a physical activity consultant for three years.

According to recent reports, in the exercise group, the target was similar to adding 45 to 60 minutes of brisk walking, three to four times a week. The amount and type of activity varied from person to person, remarked Tormod Skogstad Nilsen, a cancer exercise researcher in Norway. But he said participants achieved lasting increases in their physical activity.

Exercise helped. People in the exercise group were less likely to see their cancer come back, to develop a new cancer or to die. In all, 93 had at least one of these setbacks, compared with 131 in the health education group.

Sources indicate that in cancer research, living longer usually means a larger share of people is still alive at a given point. It does not promise anyone a set number of extra years.

Eight years after joining CHALLENGE, about 90 of every 100 people in the exercise group were alive, compared with about 83 of every 100 in the health education group. That is about 7% more people alive in the group who had guided exercise.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Recent findings suggest that for people without cancer, the evidence comes from studies that follow people's habits and health over many years. These can show a link, but not prove cause and effect. Active people may also eat better or smoke less.

In another 2025 study, more than 85,000 adults in the United Kingdom wore a wrist tracker for a week. Over about six years, those who moved most had a 26% lower risk of 13 cancers, including breast and colorectal cancer, than those who moved least.

Sources indicate that even light activity, such as household chores, was linked to lower risk. The link held after researchers accounted for lifestyle, weight and other health conditions.

It has been revealed that earlier research, based on people's self-reporting, has led to similar conclusions. A 2016 analysis of 1.44 million adults in the US and Europe linked free-time activity to a lower risk of many cancers, largely regardless of weight or smoking.

A trial to prove prevention is unlikely: Many cancers take years to develop, so it would need huge numbers of people followed for a long time.

CHALLENGE included only people with colon cancer. But how it picked participants offers a clue: Before joining, they had to pass a fitness test.

Anna Campbell, a professor of clinical exercise science at Edinburgh Napier University in Scotland, sees that as a guide.

It has been revealed that "I think patients with any other cancer stage II and III who have a reasonable baseline level of fitness and no major comorbidities that would prevent them from undertaking moderate to vigorous activity could be considered for similar interventions," she noted. Comorbidities are other health conditions.

It has been revealed that nilsen noted some people decline to join exercise trials because they feel too unwell or tired, or do not want to exercise. "Hence, study populations are typically younger, 'healthier', and most times slightly more motivated compared to a clinical population," he said.

The coaching aimed to make activity a lasting habit, and Campbell stated that is where the trial's value lies.

"The main success of the study is that it enabled the participants to become independent exercisers staying active in a safe and effective and individualized way," she said.

Nilsen agreed. Helping people become more active "in their own environment," without depending on a well-equipped training center, "would likely lead to more sustainable activity behavioral changes," he said.

He is wary of fixed targets, however. "Exercise should be tailored to each individual and the challenges they face, rather than striving to reach a given minimum of exercise required," though health care resources may not always allow it, he added.

In a 2024 survey of 549 people with cancer, only one in 10 had been referred to an exercise service. Yet almost three in four thought their oncologist should raise the subject.

"There are some excellent examples of effective pathways but these are few and far between," said Campbell. Good services bring everyone on board, from surgeons to community fitness instructors.

"Ideally, one person in the clinical setting needs to champion the program to link all the team together.".

Campbell expects CHALLENGE's regular coaching will be cut back in everyday care. Apps and live online group sessions could still work, she mentioned, if run by properly trained staff.

One recent study of live online exercise engaged patients from poorer backgrounds, in rural areas and with advanced cancer. "It answered some of the barriers, such as cost, travel and lack of confidence," she noted.

Patients can ask their care team what exercise is safe for them and what support exists.

According to Nilsen, a training session can bring structure and manufacturer. "You made it here, despite your feeling unwell or fatigued this morning, so you feel mastery based on that," he stated.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Since its inception in 1990, the Women's Ice Hockey World Championship has almost always been held in the spring — apart from 2021 and 2022, when the COVID-19 pandemic saw it moved to the summer.
  • According to recent reports, the idea is make it easier for all of the world's best players to participate.
  • It has been revealed that "This gives the women's game a unique selling point," International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) President Franz Reindl recently told the SID news agency.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Since its inception in 1990, the Women's Ice Hockey World Championship has almost always been held in the spring — apart from 2021 and 2022, when the COVID-19 pandemic saw it moved to the summer. This year, though, the tournament, being hosted by Denmark from November 6 to November 16, is being held in November for the first time.

According to recent reports, the idea is make it easier for all of the world's best players to participate. Since its inception in 2023, the North America-based Professional Women's Hockey League (PWHL), widely considered the world's best, has had to pause its season to allow players to take part in the Worlds. This is no longer necessary, as the PWHL's regular season doesn't open until December.

It has been revealed that "This gives the women's game a unique selling point," International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) President Franz Reindl recently told the SID news agency. "Because the PWHL season begins after this, we can be certain that the very best players are participating.".

Industry observers note that previously, the teams were divided into a stronger group and a weaker group, with the idea being to avoid, as much as possible, lopsided scores. This is because women's hockey is not as balanced as the men's game, with Canada or the United States having won every tournament since its inception.

Under the old system, all five teams in the stronger Group A advanced to the quarterfinals. Under the latest format, four of the five teams advance from both groups. This also sees powerhouses the US and Canada in separate groups, meaning the marquee matchup can't occur early in the tournament.

Group A: USA, Czechia, Switzerland, Germany, Austria.

Group B: Canada, Finland, Sweden, Japan, Denmark.

No. While the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruled on October 30 — a week before the opening faceoff of the Women's Ice Hockey World Championship — that the IIHF must allow Russia back into its tournaments during the 2026-2027 season, it made no mention of this tournament. Under the CAS ruling though, the IIHF will be required to include Russia at the 2027 tournament in Quebec City.

As noted above, either Canada or the United States has won every edition of this tournament — and indeed the two countries have split Olympic gold medals between them (Canada with five, USA with three) since the sport was introduced to the Winter Games in 1998. There is nothing to suggest that this is about to change in Herning and Esbjerg, although Canada enters the tournament with a vastly different roster from the one that won Olympic silver in Milano in February.

Among those looking to break this North American domination are Finland, the only other team ever to have made it to a world championship final and Switzerland, who took bronze in Milan.

The United States and Canada will play in generic kits provided by the International Ice Hockey Federation's official supplier due to an ongoing commercial rights dispute.

Industry observers note that the Canadian federation, Hockey Canada, said in a statement on Wednesday that its players would be wearing jerseys designed by True Hockey instead of their Bauer jerseys featuring the national team logo. USA Hockey has confirmed that its players too will be wearing jerseys without its national emblem.

"While we have yet to see the jersey Canada will be playing in on Friday, our team remains focused on the tournament and representing our country proudly on and off the ice," Hockey Canada remarked.

After Arsenal were beaten by Bayern Munich in a Champions League quarter-final two years ago, Mikel Arteta bemoaned a lack of “magic moments” in attack.

Arsenal have since progressed to a Champions League semi-final and final, while ending a 22-year wait for a Premier League title.

The upward trajectory has translated to tangible success, but Arsenal are still searching the level-raising attacker they lacked on their last visit to the Allianz Arena in 2024.

Back then, Arsenal’s offensive game revolved around Kai Havertz, Bukayo Saka and Martin Odegaard and that remains the case, which makes one wonder if Arsenal’s forward options have been adequately renewed.

A pair of stodgy performances (in victory) against Leeds United and Nottingham Forest have amplified those questions, though some of Arsenal’s slicker football in the season’s early weeks has been forgotten a little hastily.

They have made another strong start to another European campaign with six points from six, but this is undoubtedly their hardest fixture of the league phase.

Their chances of matching last season’s eight wins from eight could well hinge on the outcome of tonight’s game, but there are worse times to face Bayern.

Vincent Kompany’s team looks as formidable as ever, having scored 22 goals from six Bundesliga games so far this season. Their rotational approach is hard to track, with runners from deep breaking beyond Harry Kane who wanders into deep midfield positions.

However, they are without Michael Olise (suspension) and Jamal Musiala (injury) while Joshua Kimmich will miss the game on compassionate grounds following the death of his father.

With the exception of William Saliba, Christos Tzolis and Piero Hincacpie, Arsenal have a pretty clean bill of health and the strength of their bench was crucial against Leeds, Lille and Forest last week.

For Arteta, there are some interesting selection calls to make. Should Arteta continue that policy, Myles Lewis-Skelly will fill the position, which will likely mean a midfield start for Bruno Guimarães or Mikel Merino.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Imagine a situation in which prolonged drought has devastated Germany and much of Europe, taking a toll on people's lives, the environment and economy — with a heat wave with temperatures of up to 45 degrees Celsius (113 degrees Fahrenheit) compounding the situation.

About 180 organizations across Germany, including more than 60 ministries at the state level and nearly 20 federal authorities, are taking part in a major crisis exercise known as LÜKEX 26, which is built around this very scenario.

Industry observers note that it is Germany's cross-government crisis management exercise organized by the Federal Office of Civil Protection and Disaster Assistance (BBK). And it's been up and running for more than two decades.

The first LÜKEX in 2004 dealt with the scenario of an extreme winter with a major power outage. Lessons from that exercise proved valuable in 2005 when the Münsterland region of North Rhine-Westphalia — Germany's most populous state — experienced the worst power outage in the country's postwar history. When heavy snowfall caused power lines to collapse, leaving 250,000 people without electricity for days, there was a better understanding of who to contact and where the bottlenecks were.

Since it first started, LÜKEX has trained for scenarios involving terror attacks, an influenza pandemic, biological health threats, storm floods in northern Germany and gas shortages in southern Germany. The most recent exercise in 2023 simulated a cyberattack targeting government operations.

With the help of other ministries, the German Weather Service and the Federal Institute of Hydrology, the BBK developed a drought risk analysis to serve as the scenario.

Participants, which include aid organizations Malteser and the German Red Cross, didn't know the specifics of the challenges they would be facing until the exercise kicked off on Wednesday.

At that point, they were told it was July 20, 2027. In that simulated future, they find themselves in a Germany that has been struggling with extreme heat for weeks; water levels in rivers are falling, food supplies are becoming scarce and emergency services are under growing pressure.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Recent findings suggest that patrick Pöhler, spokesperson for Malteser, stated additional details include supermarkets having run out of water, collapsed supply chains and skyrocketing prices to enter a swimming pool. He said the scenario also goes into how the situation is impacting sections of society.

In a recent development, "Emergency services and elderly care are areas that require particular attention," Pöhler said. "The increasingly extreme summers of recent years have shown how severely heat can affect staffing levels and operational capacity.".

In its scenario, the northern port city of Hamburg is tasked with managing the disruption of key transport routes that are impacting access to food and drinking water, as well as handling disinformation attacks that are fueling public fear.

"We have not conducted an exercise of this magnitude since the end of the Cold War. Yet such preparations are essential to strengthen our resilience and crisis-response capabilities," mentioned Hamburg's minister for the interior, Andy Grote.

In a recent development, LÜKEX is designed to test and strengthen the country's ability to manage major crises at a strategic level. No matter the specific scenario, they all help test internal structures, workflows and decision-making processes.

"The lessons learned are continuously incorporated into improving preparedness, planning and cooperation in civil protection," said BBK spokesperson Katharina Böcker.

Sources indicate that this year's topic was decided a long time ago, well before recent summers in which Germany experienced extreme heat, she added. Thousands of people died from heat-related causes during the hot months of this year.

"Crises such as extreme heat waves and prolonged droughts can affect large parts of the population and challenge the operational capabilities of our critical structures over an extended period," remarked Christian Reuter, secretary general of the German Red Cross, another organization taking part.

Observers take note of how organizations react in the crisis scenario to find out what went well and where things didn't run smoothly.

"We are explicitly encouraged to make mistakes," remarked Malteser's Pöhler, because that is how weaknesses can be identified and addressed.

A first internal debrief is scheduled for Friday, he added.

According to recent reports, A preliminary report with the main findings and respective recommendations is due to be published in the first quarter of next year. A full evaluation report will then be released later in the third quarter of 2027.

  • Everton tasted their first defeat in the Subway Players Cup as the Blues' four-game winning streak in the competition came to its conclusion with a 2-1 defeat away to Manchester United.
  • First half strikes from Mared Griffiths and Emma Watson put the Red Devils in to a two-goal lead, before Noemie Mouchon halved the deficit two minutes after the break.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Everton tasted their first defeat in the Subway Players Cup as the Blues' four-game winning streak in the competition came to its conclusion with a 2-1 defeat away to Manchester United.

First half strikes from Mared Griffiths and Emma Watson put the Red Devils in to a two-goal lead, before Noemie Mouchon halved the deficit two minutes after the break.

Prior to Wednesday night's clash, the Toffees had comfortably beaten Birmingham City, Newcastle United and Sheffield United before thrashing Durham 6-0 in the competition.

Head coach Scott Phelan named a heavily-rotated XI from the side that were held to a goalless draw against Tottenham Hotspur on Saturday.

Rylee Foster-Inman started in between the sticks, with Issy Hobson making her first appearance in two months in front of her.

Up top, Mouchon led the line after netting a brace in the Blues’ 6-0 demolition of Durham seven days ago.

Sources indicate that foster-Inman produced a fine save when faced one-on-one with Griffiths inside six minutes. The keeper rushed out upon recognising the danger and did brilliantly to narrow the angle.

The shot-stopper denied Griffiths once more on 21 minutes as the youngster pulled the trigger from the edge of the box after a cute turn saw her evade Hobson.

Recent findings suggest that the lively Griffiths was in the thick of the action once more in the 34th minute as United came inches away from opening the scoring. Rebecca Bernal burst forward to meet her in swinging cross, the Mexican’s header sailing just over.

Griffiths would not be denied only 60 seconds later as the forward broke the deadlock in style. She sprinted down the left before chopping past Finnigan and firing past the outrushed Foster-Inman.

Watson then doubled the hosts’ lead on the stroke of half-time. Ella Toone wrong-footed Finnigan before pulling it back to the former-Blue. Watson finished emphatically from close range, with that concluding the action for the opening 45.

Defensive duo Hobson and Silcock made way for Hannah Blundell and Rion Ishikawa at the break.

Sources indicate that everton halved the deficit only 60 seconds after the restart as Mouchon netted her third goal from her last two Cup appearances. Quick feet from Vignola allowed the Spaniard room to free Hannah Cain down the right. The Wales international then squared it to the advancing Mouchon, who finished off the post.

According to recent reports, maz Pacheco then came agonisingly close from 20-yards out as her wicked free-kick rattled the upright. The full-back picked her spot from the set-piece – the ball crashing against the crossbar with the keeper well-beaten.

Phelan then made two further changes on 68 minutes as Ruby Mace and Hikaru Kitagawa replaced Clare Wheeler and Vignola.

With eight minutes remaining, Naomi Layzell – who claimed the Player of the Match award when the two sides met in the WSL – came on in place of Aurora Galli.

Despite a late push for an equaliser, United stood firm and succumbed the Toffees to their first defeat in the Subway Players Cup.

Everton return to Goodison Park on Sunday afternoon (2pm KO) as Brighton & Hove Albion travel to L4.

Tesla to 'wind down' production of flop Cybertruck

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (673 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tesla owner Elon Musk said on Friday that the company would scale down production of the Cybertruck at its Austin factory in the coming year.
  • The South African entrepreneur noted Tesla would be scaling back production of his futuristic but often-mocked pickup truck and amping up production of what he hopes will soon become a fleet of fully automated taxis.
  • "Tesla will be winding down production of the cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production," Musk stated on his X social media site.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tesla owner Elon Musk said on Friday that the company would scale down production of the Cybertruck at its Austin factory in the coming year.

The South African entrepreneur noted Tesla would be scaling back production of his futuristic but often-mocked pickup truck and amping up production of what he hopes will soon become a fleet of fully automated taxis.

"Tesla will be winding down production of the cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production," Musk stated on his X social media site.

The announcement follows a bruising week for Musk amid the US midterm elections, where Republicans struggled despite his major donations, with his companies losing billions in value by market capitalization as investors sought to ditch stock.

Musk later responded to a complimentary user online who hailed the Cybertruck as the "best vehicle Tesla has ever made," and calling it an "end of an era" by saying: "True.".

For years he had poured much of his enthusiastic marketing zeal into promoting the Cybertruck, saying during the 2023 launch "finally, the future will look like the future.".

However the oversized body, straight lines and stainless steel and the post-apocalpytic vibe these created also met with widespread criticism and even mockery.

The electric powertrain was probably a barrier to sales in the US, by far the biggest pickup truck market, where Musk had hoped to take on some of the country's top-selling gas-guzzling vehicles like the Ford F150 or the Chevrolet Silverado and the Dodge Ram.

Meanwhile, the car's striking shape, weight and size made it impossible for Tesla to try to crack Europe, where electric vehicles are gaining a much larger market share.

According to recent reports, unlike in the US, EU safety regulations place considerable emphasis not just on people in cars in accidents, but also on the dangers posed to pedestrians who might be hit by a vehicle. That meant it was not possible for Tesla to register and sell the Cybertruck for road use in Europe.

Beyond this, the vehicle's size would likely have rendered it impractical and unpopular on many European roads, where space tends to be at more of a premium.

Depending how quick the wind-down proves to be, the Cybertruck's production run could prove shorter than its five-year R&D phase.

Given its longstanding concerns meeting Musk's very public sales and production predictions, Tesla does not publish sales figures broken down by model.

But according to the automotive data platform Kelley Blue Book, the tech giant sold 20,237 Cybertrucks in the US last year, down from 38,965 in 2024.

At launch in 2023, Musk had predicted unit sales nearer a quarter of a million.

For orientation, Ford sold more than 800,000 F-Series pickups in the US last year, a slight boost on 2024's numbers. These vehicles start at less than half the list price of a Cybertruck in the US.

The IPO for SpaceX this year revealed that Musk's second-largest company was comfortably the biggest buyer of Cybertrucks in 2025. It bought vehicles worth $131 million and did not even enjoy a bulk-buy or friends-rate discount, paying list prices for the fleet.

The Cybercab is a vehicular element in Musk's bid to transform Tesla towards a firm focused more on AI and robotics than automobilies.

Rather than just featuring the self-drive or driving assistance programs that Musk has been championing for years, the Cybercab has no steering wheels, pedals or mirrors at all and is designed never to have a human in control.

Musk say the model will be the organization's main autonomous model and will supply a global network of Robotaxis.

Starting in the past few months, around 300 such vehicles have been registered and have started operating, on approved roads in the Austin area near Tesla's Gigafactory Texas. They're being added to the existing fleet of autonomous Model Y Teslas being used for the purpose, serving in an area known as a geofence of around 680 square kilometers (264 square miles).

Band-Edge-Extended Heterointerfaces for Perovskite Solar Cells and Tandems

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (739 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Perovskite solar cells (PSCs) have emerged as a promising photovoltaic technology, with efficiencies rapidly approaching those of established crystalline-silicon solar cells.
  • This is a preview of subscription content, access via your institution.
  • Access Nature and 54 other Nature Portfolio journals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Perovskite solar cells (PSCs) have emerged as a promising photovoltaic technology, with efficiencies rapidly approaching those of established crystalline-silicon solar cells. Further efficiency gains, however, are increasingly limited by charge extraction and recombination at the interface between the perovskite absorber and the electron-transport layer. Interfacial modifiers are widely used to suppress these losses, yet many conventional ammonium-based modifiers are weakly electronically coupled to the perovskite surface and can introduce barriers to electron extraction 1-5. Here we realize electronically coupled heterointerfaces by introducing a family of heteroatom-containing, fully conjugated formamidinium interfacial modulators, establishing band-edge-extending conjugated heterointerfaces that overcome the bottleneck of inefficient interfacial electron transfer. The resulting band-edge-extended heterointerface establishes delocalized electron connectivity at the perovskite/electron transporting layer (ETL) interface and suppresses interfacial non-radiative recombination. We report a certified power-conversion efficiency (PCE) of 27.96% and a stabilized power output (SPO) of 27.84% for inverted PSCs. The corresponding devices retained over 95% of their initial efficiency after 2000 h continuous maximum-power-point tracking under 1-sun irradiation (ISOS-L). Extending this strategy to monolithic perovskite–silicon tandems enables a certified SPO of 34.71%, establishing band-edge extension as a broadly applicable approach to overcoming the conventional trade-off between interfacial passivation and charge extraction.

KILMARNOCK 2 ABERDEEN 4: Dazzling Dons get a Frick pick-up but it's more misery for McCann's men

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (966 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dailymail

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Published: 15:33 EST, 21 November 2026 | Updated: 16:15 EST, 21 November 2026.
  • Having been bored senseless by the football offered up under Stephen Robinson, Aberdeen supporters were – at the very least – crying out for the next appointment to provide some sort of entertainment to get excited about over the dark winter months.
  • Sources indicate that in Mario Frick, they may have got their man.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Published: 15:33 EST, 21 November 2026 | Updated: 16:15 EST, 21 November 2026.

Having been bored senseless by the football offered up under Stephen Robinson, Aberdeen supporters were – at the very least – crying out for the next appointment to provide some sort of entertainment to get excited about over the dark winter months.

Sources indicate that in Mario Frick, they may have got their man. Whether or not the former Luzern boss will be a success at Pittodrie is anyone’s guess. But on this evidence, it’s going to be a lot of fun watching him have a go.

At times, they were scintillating here on their way to a thrilling win which moved them five clear of their hosts and provided some much-needed breathing room ahead of a tricky upcoming schedule which involves trips to Ibrox and Tynecastle, as well as two home clashes against the Dundee clubs.

Industry observers note that yes, it wasn’t perfect. Far from it, in fact. Defensively, they were far too open. Kilmarnock just weren’t good enough to take full advantage.

But you suspect that will be forgiven to an extent as long as they can play with this level of panache and aggression going forward.

Findlay Marshall celebrates after scoring the Dons' fourth goal at Rugby Park.

Frick has arrived with the promise of bringing ‘heavy metal’ football to Pittodrie. It’s taken a little over 90 minutes to understand what he's talking about.

In a recent development, ‘It was very chaotic,’ he admitted. ‘It's quite different to Switzerland, because there is technicality, but it’s not as physical as it was today.

‘It was difficult. We were lucky as well because Killie, especially in the second half, played very well, but I think at the end it's a deserved victory.

‘When the players were young, they didn’t think about mistakes, didn’t think about any negatives.

‘They played only to win for fun, and I told them to play as if they were young players and I think, especially first half, it was very good.

‘You don't know what's going on or what can happen in this first game, so I'm very happy we won.’.

Frick shows his delight after tasting victory in his first match in charge of Aberdeen.

Kilmarnock spurned a golden opportunity to take a sixth-minute lead at the end of a rapid counter-attack, with Joe Hugill finding himself all alone in the Dons box.

In a recent development, the striker took a heavy first touch, allowing Marius Muller to swiftly narrow the angle and block the effort. It’s easy to see why Hugill has found the back of the net just twice this year.

And the hosts were made to pay for that miss within 90 seconds as Aberdeen went in front.

In a recent development, for the umpteenth time this season, Killie failed to clear their lines under little pressure, with Stuart Armstrong teeing up Kevin Nisbet to sweep home a lovely finish from the edge of the area. The unsighted Nico Mantl in the Killie goal didn’t even move.

Mind you, he should have done significantly better four minutes later as Nisbet notched his second of the afternoon.

The keeper’s positioning as the Dons striker stepped up to send a low free-kick in off the post was as poor as it gets.

You got the feeling that the walls would have caved in had Aberdeen grabbed a third, but a brief drop-off in intensity from Frick’s side enabled Killie to drag themselves back into the contest.

A bit of pinball outside the Dons box saw the ball fall favourably for skipper Greg Kiltie 12 yards out, who adjusted his body brilliantly to drill beyond Muller on the half-volley.

Yet with a defence as dodgy as this, manager Neil McCann can never feel overly confident.

Ante Palaversa – terrific on his first appearance of the season – was given far too much time in the centre circle to get his head up and pick out Nesta Guinness-Walker on the left.

He glided past MJ Kamson-Kamara as if he wasn’t there before dinking a ball right on to the head of Brad Lyons, who rose completely unopposed to power home against his former employers.

If Killie continue to defend like this, relegation is a certainty. Will the manager even get the chance to turn it around? Going off the abuse being hurled in his direction from the home punters, his jacket is evidently on a shoogly peg. Many fans have already made up their mind.

Nisbet's free-kick finds the net for his second as the Dons take control of the game.

Michael Schjonning-Larsen’s deflected effort from 20 yards shortly after the restart looked destined for the goal before Muller instinctively leapt to his right to claw it away on the line. It was a superb stop.

His next contribution defied belief.

Goodness knows what the keeper was thinking as he tried to pass out from the six-yard line, playing it straight to the feet of Tyreece John-Jules – only just on the park – who steadied himself before finishing.

You would have stuck your house on Nisbet putting this one to bed with five minutes remaining, however with just Mantl to beat, he pulled his left-footed effort wide.

Findlay Marshall showed him how it’s done with stoppage-time looming, running half the length of the field before drilling low into the corner to consign Killie to another sobering defeat.

McCann remarked: ‘I probably sound like a broken record, but we create really substantial, big chances, and we don't take them.

Industry observers note that ‘We're letting games pass us by. We're giving teams the opportunity to start ahead of us because of the goals we're conceding and then it's difficult to work back.’.

#83130. Amid protests, France's rising debt costs threaten stability

📅 06 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (987 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

Amid protests, France's rising debt costs threaten stability

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (987 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Deeply indebted, politically trapped in a standoff between extremes and led by a government without a parliamentary majority: These are the defining features of France's current predicament.
  • If, in response to nationwide protests, the government plans to provide €4 billion ($4.48 billion) in low-interest loans to renovate schools by 2030 and allocate a further €1 billion to universities by 2029, it is promising money the state simply does not have.
  • France's public debt stands at around 120% of gross domestic product (GDP).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Deeply indebted, politically trapped in a standoff between extremes and led by a government without a parliamentary majority: These are the defining features of France's current predicament.

If, in response to nationwide protests, the government plans to provide €4 billion ($4.48 billion) in low-interest loans to renovate schools by 2030 and allocate a further €1 billion to universities by 2029, it is promising money the state simply does not have.

France's public debt stands at around 120% of gross domestic product (GDP). By comparison, Germany's debt-to-GDP ratio is roughly 65%, despite its €600 billion investment package for infrastructure and defense.

Germany still enjoys the highest possible AAA credit rating. France, by contrast, is rated AA, A+ or Aa3, depending on the credit agency. While Germany's outlook is consistently rated as stable, several agencies have assigned France a negative outlook.

Industry observers note that as a result, the French government must pay higher interest rates on its borrowing than Berlin. The risk premium over German government bonds, known as the spread, is now at its highest level since the financial crisis. France pays nearly 1.6 percentage points more in interest than Germany on 10-year bonds.

The spread acts as a kind of "fever gauge" for bond markets, explained Friedrich Heinemann, an economist at the Leibniz Center for European Economic Research (ZEW) in Mannheim.

"This fever gauge then forces a change of course. If the spread rises too sharply, France's financing conditions come under pressure, and anyone in France who needs a loan has to pay higher interest rates. Banks then get into trouble, and the crisis escalates further," Heinemann told DW.

"This could then slide toward a financial crisis, which would finally send a clear signal to everyone: Things cannot continue like this unless you are prepared to risk a genuine economic collapse," he stated.

Landry Charrier, a researcher at the University of Bonn's Center for Advanced Security, Strategic and Integration Studies, however, does not expect France's debt-fueled spending spree to end anytime soon.

"French people are aware of the country's high public debt. But debt remains an abstract concept if its consequences are barely felt in everyday life. According to INSEE [the French national statistics agency — Editor's note], 56% of the population receive more in government benefits and services than they pay in taxes and social contributions. The majority therefore have a tangible interest in maintaining the status quo," Charrier told DW.

According to recent reports, for more than half a century, France has regularly spent more than it collects in tax revenue. The last time it balanced its national budget was in 1974.

It has been revealed that france last paid a similarly high-risk premium at the end of 2011, during the eurozone debt crisis. What is particularly striking is how promptly it has risen: Since June 2026, the spread over German government bonds has more than doubled.

The main driver is not so much the general level of interest rates. Rather, it's the growing risk premium investors demand in response to high debt levels, political instability, large budget deficits and the recent unrest.

The higher the interest rates, the larger the share of the national budget that must be devoted to debt servicing alone. France is expected to pay more than €79 billion in interest on its total public debt in 2026. That figure is projected to exceed €91 billion in 2027 and could reach between €125 billion and €132 billion by 2030.

These figures include the costs incurred by social security funds and local authorities. The central government's interest bill alone is at the moment estimated at €62.6 billion by the Agence France Tresor, a French Treasury agency.

It has been revealed that in the coming years, France will have to refinance large amounts of outstanding bonds that were issued when interest rates were at historic lows. At the same time, the country's substantial budget deficit means it must take on additional debt.

The trend of rising interest costs is also affecting Germany. The ZEW's Heinemann has calculated that German interest payments are likely to increase sharply by the early 2030s.

"For the federal government alone, which has so far paid around €30 billion, the figure will triple within a few years as both debt and interest rates rise. And it won't stop there — it will exceed €90 billion. Reaching €100 billion in annual interest payments in the federal budget is then no longer far off," warned the economist.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

In a recent development, in France, however, economic realities seem to have little impact on political debate. Both the far-right National Rally (RN) and the far-left France Unbowed (LFI) are campaigning on costly promises.

RN leader Marine Le Pen, for example, wants to reinstate the retirement age of 62 while promising €140 billion in savings. Jean-Luc Melenchon, LFI's leader, has even suggested that government bonds held by the French central bank should be "thrown into the fire.".

"Nobody will ever notice they've disappeared," he has claimed.

For Heinemann, this is "a good example of radical parties on both the right and the left simply telling economic fairy tales.".

Their common message, he said, is that "there is a way out of this mess that requires neither fiscal consolidation nor painful cuts.".

Charrier is convinced that many French people have yet to grasp the seriousness of the situation.

"The euro has made it easier for France to access cheap financing and has long softened the pressure to adjust," he pointed out.

"In the past, currency devaluations [of the French franc — Editor's note] made economic imbalances immediately felt through declining purchasing power and rising prices. Today, that warning signal is missing. This has created the illusion that necessary adjustments can be postponed indefinitely," Charrier said.

This article was originally written in German.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A government spokesman has said that, despite talks with the German Ice Hockey Federation (DEB), the International Ice Hockey Federation (DEB) and others, the impasse caused by last week's Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruling remains.

Sources indicate that since the October 30 decision, several leading ice hockey nations — including Finland, Sweden and Czechia — have said they would refrain from playing against Russia in any tournament in which it is allowed to take part. Several key sponsors have also threatened to pull out, should the Russians be allowed to play.

The first tournament to be affected would be the Men's World Juniors, which opens in Canada in late December, followed by the IIHF's premier event, the Men's World Ice Championship, to be hosted by Germany in May.

Stefan Kornelius, the spokesman for Germany's government, told reporters in Berlin on Friday that talks held with various stakeholders had made clear that Russia's participation would render the hosting of the championship "practically impossible — both from a sporting and an economic perspective.".

Kornelius stated talks would continue and the government still hoped for a diplomatic solution that would allow Germany to host the championship — as planned — in Gelsenkirchen, Mannheim and Düsseldorf in May.

In a recent development, "Our goal must be to hold the tournaments as scheduled," he said. "However, given the boycotts that would follow Russia's readmission, that would effectively be impossible. For this reason, we intend to explore — through dialogue — how we can still ensure the tournament takes place.".

Following the CAS ruling that the IIHF must allow Russia to return to international play, DEB chairman Frank Lutz had conceded that Germany may be forced to consider withdrawing as championship host.

Asked at Friday's press conference whether Germany could problem visas to a Russian team for the tournament, a Foreign Ministry spokesman declined to answer categorically, but did indicate that this would be difficult under restrictions right now in place.

"At a time when Russia is waging a war of aggression against Ukraine, there can be no 'normalcy' — and we will certainly not pretend that there is," mentioned spokesperson Martin Giese.

Earlier this week, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney categorically ruled out Russian players taking part in the World Juniors in Alberta.

"While Russia and Belarus are supporting this illegal, unjustified ​war in Ukraine, as long as that's going on, there will be none of those athletes competing for their countries in Canada," he remarked.

"So, ​if you're asking specifically about the World Juniors," he said, "the Russians will not be there.".

Russian President Vladimir Putin has also weighed in on the issue, accusing countries opposing Russia's return to international sport of violating the rights of his country's athletes.

The IIHF Council had originally called two days of meetings, on Monday and Tuesday, to try to reach a consensus on how to respond to the CAS decision — before extending discussions for a third day, on Thursday. By Friday, its members had evidently still not reached a consensus.

This comes as the Women's Ice Hockey World Championship, which is not affected by the CAS decision, opened in Denmark — and with the clock ticking toward the start of the World Juniors in Alberta on December 26.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hundreds of millions of people around the world are affected by diabetes mellitus1. It develops when the activity of insulin, a glucose-lowering hormone secreted by pancreatic β-cells, becomes insufficient to maintain healthy glucose levels in the blood. The condition can be managed with oral medication or by injecting insulin and other metabolic hormones, but the constant need for people with diabetes to manage their lifestyle and blood-glucose levels can impair their quality of life. Therapeutic approaches that monitor and control blood glucose automatically are therefore highly desirable. Writing in Nature, Xiu et al.2 report proof of principle of a bioelectronic device called NeuroAxis that does exactly that in rat models of diabetes.

#83125. As COP31 Antalya kicks off, can world move beyond big promises?

📅 08 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1232 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

As COP31 Antalya kicks off, can world move beyond big promises?

📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1232 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With its pulsing music, flashy images and barrage of special effects, the key message in Antalya's marketing video is clear: Turkey, the host of the 31st edition of the UN climate talks, is cool, stylish, modern — and eco-conscious.
  • Both President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and his wife, Emine, make an appearance, with Turkey's first lady calling climate change "one of the most visible manifestations of the burden human activity has placed on our planet.".
  • It has been revealed that from November 9-20, delegates from nearly every country in the world are coming together in the Mediterranean city of Antalya to chart a way out of the climate crisis.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With its pulsing music, flashy images and barrage of special effects, the key message in Antalya's marketing video is clear: Turkey, the host of the 31st edition of the UN climate talks, is cool, stylish, modern — and eco-conscious.

Both President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and his wife, Emine, make an appearance, with Turkey's first lady calling climate change "one of the most visible manifestations of the burden human activity has placed on our planet.".

It has been revealed that from November 9-20, delegates from nearly every country in the world are coming together in the Mediterranean city of Antalya to chart a way out of the climate crisis. Turkey is the official host, and Australia will lead the negotiations. But the issues they'll confront during those 12 days are far more serious than the showy marketing campaign make them out to be.

Severe drought, extreme heat, wildfires and record-low water levels in Europe's main waterways — summer across the continent was dominated by climate emergencies.

Sources indicate that and in late August, a series of flash floods triggered by a rock-ice avalanche in Nepal and Tibet washed away entire villages, killing more than 1,400 people and leaving thousands missing. Climate experts have linked the disaster to melting ice and a warming climate.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Globally, carbon emissions are still rising: the UN has concluded that it is no longer possible to keep global temperature rise to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial levels, the goal agreed at COP21 in 2015.

The global transition away from polluting fossil fuels like coal, oil and gas will be at the center of attention in Antalya — once again. To date, there's been no consensus on whether and how to transition rapidly away from this main source of global warming.

Despite the setbacks, the world has made some progress thanks to the 2015 Paris Agreement.

David Victor, a climate expert at the University of California San Diego, pointed out that before then, the planet was hurtling toward an average temperature rise of between 3-3.5 C.

Sources indicate that if current climate commitments are fully implemented, the latest UN projections show a rise of up to 2.6 C. It's a significant step forward, even though warming of that magnitude will still have worldwide consequences.

"There's no question that we could be doing more," said Victor, though he cautioned against pinning too much on this year's summit.

It has been revealed that all agreements at COP need to be unanimous, meaning individual states can quash any sweeping resolutions. Added to that challenge are the ongoing wars, trade conflicts and other economic problems swirling around this year's negotiations.

In a recent development, "It's like a giant Christmas tree in which everybody's hung their different ornaments, and the tree is groaning and more ornaments are being put on it," mentioned Victor. "We have to look at it for what it is: It's a place where people talk about stuff.".

Instead of waiting for all COP member states to agree, Victor sees a better chance for change in what he called "clubs" — smaller alliances of governments and companies working together to advance actual solutions, whether it be in aviation, shipping or electromobility.

According to recent reports, "The Paris process is key. It has to go forward," he told DW. "But all the work is going to be done in clubs.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

An example of this approach was last April's first ever International Conference on Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels in Santa Marta, Colombia.

Colombia and the Netherlands invited representatives from 57 countries and key sectors to discuss ways to move the world away from coal, oil and gas, after an agreement on a similar proposal failed at the 2025 climate summit due to opposition from several oil-producing states.

With an eye to the ongoing trade conflicts and energy crisis, hosts Turkey and Australia have included green industrialization and the clean energy transition among their aims. One goal is to increase the share of electricity in global energy consumption to 35% by 2035, up from around 20% today.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Industry observers note that A recent analysis by the International Energy Agency found accelerating electrification could cut fuel-importing countries' energy bills by more than $400 billion (€357 billion) by 2035, compared to 2025 levels. The idea could appeal to regions dependent on fossil fuel imports — among them Germany and the European Union.

Ahead of COP31, German Environment Minister Carsten Schneider said Germany and the EU wanted to spark latest momentum in the "global phaseout of fossil fuels.".

It's wouldn't just be good for the climate, but a chance for many countries to boost their economies and reduce dependence on energy imports, added Schneider in a statement.

Sources indicate that oil-producing states like Saudi Arabia, however, aren't interested in deals that will undermine their business model. At recent UN climate conferences, they've repeatedly blocked any final agreements, including phaseout plans.

According to recent reports, even China, despite its massive expansion of wind and solar energy over the last 20 years, could be against the idea. The economic superpower traditionally rejects any outside demands, proposals or interference concerning its national decisions on energy policy.

Every country in the world is affected by climate change, with loss and damage calculated in the hundreds of billions from heat, drought and storms. Worst hit are vulnerable countries in the Global South and island nations, who are at risk of disappearing as sea levels rise.

That's where money comes into play, with developing countries calling for more support to protect their citizens from the harms of global warming. At the 2024 UN climate talks in Baku, Azerbaijan, industrialized nations agreed to free up at least $300 billion annually in climate financing by 2035.

But where exactly all those funds will come from remains hotly debated. At the same time, several major developed countries — most notably, the US — have cut their development aid.

The German government only paid out €4.7 billion from its 2025 budget for international climate financing, down from €6.1 billion in 2024.

"The level of financial support for developing countries today is far from what's needed," said Jan Kowalzig, a climate expert at Oxfam Germany.

Breaking financial promises like this comes at the expense of losing the trust of developing countries and, as a result, the diplomatic power which Germany and other industrialized nations rely on to shape policy to fight climate change.

Cosima Cassel, who focuses on climate diplomacy at the independent think tank E3G in Berlin, believes Turkey's push to turbocharge electrification during an oil crisis could be successful.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

For Cassel, a successful outcome at what are expected to be difficult negotiations in Antalya would reveal actual political will behind the grand agreements.

When it comes to electrification, that means taking the expansion of electricity grids and battery storage capacity seriously — not to mention removing the barriers to further electrification.

Enzo Maresca’s flawless start to the Premier League with Manchester City is over after another masterclass from Unai Emery.

On his fourth anniversary in charge of Villa, there was more tactical brilliance from Emery, who also did the double over Guardiola last season. It was Emery’s £65m record signing Nicolas Jackson who again underlined how some managers can get the best out of certain players.

Jackson had been a target for Emery ever since the Basque’s appointment and now has seven goals in claret and blue. It will have been an especially sweet moment for the Senegal forward, for it was Maresca who allowed him to join Bayern Munich on loan while he was in charge at Chelsea.

City’s run of seven league wins in a row always looked in danger here against a vibrant and energetic Villa. Maresca will also reflect on two poor goals conceded after errors from Marc Guéhi and goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma.

Guéhi endured a particularly difficult afternoon and was at fault for Jackson’s stunning first goal. The centre-back has struggled in recent weeks with a bad mistake in England’s defeat by Spain and he was exposed for both Ipswich goals last week. He was replaced at half-time after a booking for a foul on the excellent Jackson.

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Aston Villa vs Manchester City.

Premier League leaders City will attempt to maintain their flawless start to the season when they visit Villa Park for Saturday’s lunchtime kick-off.

The match marks the first meeting between the sides since the final weekend of last season, when Villa secured a 2-1 victory at the Etihad in Pep Guardiola’s final game in charge at City.

Enzo Maresca became the first manager in City’s Premier League history to win his opening seven fixtures, lifting his side three points clear of title holders Arsenal. Only Chelsea in 2005-06 and Liverpool in 2019-20 have managed a longer winning start to a top-flight campaign. Following a 3-2 victory against Ipswich Town last weekend, City rebounded from a European setback against Paris Saint-Germain by delivering a commanding 5-1 Champions League win over AEK Athens on Wednesday.

In a recent development, however, Unai Emery’s side will present a formidable challenge. Aston Villa enter the contest on a seven-match unbeaten streak across all competitions, headlined by a perfect record in the Champions League following midweek success against Viking FK.

Sources indicate that villa’s domestic form has also improved, taking seven points from their last three league outings, including a 1-0 away victory at Newcastle United in Emery’s 100th Premier League match as manager. Sitting 12th in the table, Villa remain on the hunt for their first home league win of the season, though their impressive European performances at Villa Park provide significant momentum.

According to recent reports, emery’s men completed a league double over City last term, including a 1-0 win on home turf. Should Villa claim victory again on Saturday, it would mark the first time in the Premier League era that they have recorded three consecutive victories over the Manchester club.

Of course, City’s campaign remains overshadowed by the recent guilty verdict from the Premier League over financial regulations.

Three of Everton's Premier League fixtures in January – including the Merseyside derby at Anfield – have been moved for live television coverage.

The Toffees' trip to Coventry City remains on Saturday 16 January, but with an earlier kick-off time of 12.30pm (GMT), and will be shown live on TNT Sports.

The following weekend, David Moyes' side will now host Brentford at Hill Dickinson Stadium on Sunday 24 January, in a 2pm (GMT) kick-off that will be broadcast live on Sky Sports.
